headline: Wales defy lack of crowd to create ‘own buzz’ against Japan
author: Matt Lloyd

paragraphs.text: There was a time when a trip to Twickenham was a bi-annual pilgrimage for Wales fans.
Anticipation, trepidation... travelling along the M4 motorway to English rugby's headquarters was a rare and enthralling experience.
Not so in the rugby world of 2026 when Wales have played at the Allianz Stadium three times - but only once facing England.
Since the bear pit of the Six Nations, Wales have taken on both Barbarians and Japan at Twickenham in the past six months in front of painfully sparse crowds.
Fewer than 20,000 came here to watch Wales face the Barbarians in a non-Test match in June.
On Saturday against Japan, for their final match of the Nations Championship, the crowd was marginally better though the 82,000-seater stadium was still only a third full.

After three weeks in the raucous Principality Stadium, Wales head coach Steve Tandy and captain Dafydd Jenkins were all too aware they could not guarantee a crowd could provide motivation to the players.
Even before kick-off, Tandy spoke of having to find a new mindset in order to adapt to a different atmosphere with players' voices audible from the stands.
Jenkins added: "The situation is a bit difficult and obviously everyone loves playing in their home stadium, especially as we feel like we've got the best stadium and fans in the world.
"We spoke a lot about creating our own atmosphere within the group, creating that energy and buzz and I thought we [did] that really well today."
It was also perhaps asking a lot of fans to fork out more money, with tickets coasting more than £150.

After three games in Cardiff, few will have had another trip to London on their list of rugby trips, especially this close to Christmas, in miserable weather and for a fifth meeting against the some opposition in 18 months.
The result was precious few red hats or scarves in a meagre crowd whose biggest cheer came when Japan finally got on the scoreboard late on.
Tandy admitted the fixture was "tough" on fans.
"I know it's not a huge amount of travel, but it is big. Probably off the back of the last three weeks, there is unknown [over the final opponents]."
Why did Wales play in Twickenham?

The finals weekend is the climax of a new format, which repackages July and November Test fixtures and culminates in six play-off fixtures between northern and southern hemisphere sides over three days.
Some 32,000 watched Friday's games between Italy and Fiji as well as Ireland against Australia.
Sales for Saturday and Sunday's action, headlined by England v New Zealand and a South Africa v France were stronger.
But organisers faced a struggle to market the matches and get close to filling the UK's second biggest stadium given the final weekend's fixtures were only confirmed a week earlier.
"The competition is an amazing concept, I'm open-minded about that," said Tandy.

"After the first time round of this concept, I'm sure there's things that will be worked out going forward. It's been brilliant for us playing all those different nations, [though] touring was difficult in the summer.
"There was lots of things that could be grown, but the whole concept of this playing every sort of southern hemisphere team has been really cool."
Wales wing Josh Adams agreed and said he had enjoyed the new competition.
"It's been fun travelling and then having three different teams coming to us and then a final," he said.

"I'm biased that Cardiff's the better stadium but to be fair, the atmosphere was better than I expected and the pitch really held up well given the weather and we were the third game on it in two days."

Qatar had initially been slated as a potential host for the next Nations Championship finals weekend in 2028, though London, France and Spain have also expressed interest, given unrest in the Middle East.
'Make it like Ryder Cup'
Japan head coach Eddie Jones also heaped praise on the concept but believed organisers could go further to build the hemisphere rivalry, akin to golf's Ryder Cup between USA and Europe.

"We should make it into more like a Ryder Cup concept, where teams play for their own wins, but then we should really make it north versus south and put a lot more meaning to it with tallies at the end of each round," said Jones.
"But it's great for the fans and as coaches, this is as close as you get to a World Cup as you can get, perhaps even harder.
"So we should keep building on it and not be afraid to do something a little different to make rugby exciting and make people want to come."
